metadata.title: How to make Korean BBQ @ Home
metadata.description:
Here is how I prepared Korean BBQ at home for my family! My inlaws are Chinese and they enjoy this meal once in awhile. We had Beef oven roast in the fridge and wanted to do something different with it - Korean bbq! That was Hann’s idea. Everyone does Korean bbq differently according to their own taste but this is how I like to do it sometimes. If you want any recipes of the food I made, message me in the comment section! I might do a seperate cooking tuturial for you.

Where I purchased my things:
BBQ Grill - HMART
Portable gas burner - TNT (Chinese supermarket)
Bone in oven roast - Costco (we sliced it ourselves)
Korean barchan - HMART
Vegetables - HMART

nodes.plm_caption: The video captures clips of an Asian barbecue for one, two or more people. A man and woman cook the various meats and make broth. A variety of meats, vegetables, seasonings, and sauces are displayed. A soup is cooked and a grill is set up with meat cooking while people add vegetables to the grill and enjoy the food.

summary.brief: A couple and their guests prepare and enjoy a Korean‑style BBQ at home using a tabletop grill.
summary.detailed: The video opens with title cards that say “WHAT TO EXPECT – KOREAN BBQ @ HOME.” A woman and a man appear behind a glass table, pointing out plates of tofu with sauce, several small side dishes (banchan), and a large tray of raw sliced beef. A pot of Doenjang soup bubbles on a hot‑pot burner beside the table. The camera pans to a portable tabletop grill set on the glass surface, where the sliced beef, tofu, and condiment bowls are arranged. Guests gather around, pick up raw beef with chopsticks, place it on the hot grill, flip the pieces until browned, then lift the cooked meat, dip it in the samjung sauce and wrap it in lettuce or other leafy greens before eating. The soup continues to simmer while people chat and serve themselves from the assorted plates. Later, a close‑up shows a cook (the woman) using a spoon to stir pieces of meat in a black frying pan while a white plate of additional meat sits nearby. The segment ends with a series of static end‑card graphics displaying a monitor, social‑media handles, a “Subscribe” button and the text “Thanks for watching!”

action.detailed: Place the sliced beef onto the hot tabletop grill, turn it until cooked, then pick up the pieces with chopsticks, dip them in sauce, wrap them in lettuce or leaves, and eat.
action.actor: the host couple and their guests

summary.detailed: The video opens with a simple title card that reads “WHAT TO EXPECT – KOREAN BBQ @ HOME.” It then cuts to a bright kitchen where a woman with dark hair wearing a black t‑shirt and a rainbow‑patterned apron stands beside a barefoot man in a white shirt and gray pants. They are positioned next to a glass table covered with many dishes: a plate of tofu drizzled in a brown sauce and topped with green garnish, several labeled bowls of bean mixes, a plate of cooked beef ribs, a decorative plate holding sliced cooked beef, a large bowl of raw sliced beef, and a small white bowl of lettuce. The woman points at the tofu dish while the man watches. The camera pans across the arrangement, showing close‑ups of the tofu, the raw beef, and various banchan side dishes. A portable tabletop electric grill sits in the centre of the table, and behind it a pot of bubbling doenjang‑jjigae soup simmers on an induction burner, with a text overlay that reads “DOENJANG JJIGAE.” Text such as “Sliced & Ready to Grill” appears over the meat bowl. Throughout the segment, the woman (wearing a long‑sleeve purple shirt in later shots) and other diners use chopsticks to pick up pieces of tofu, meat, and vegetables, placing them onto the hot grill, turning them as they sizzle, and dipping them in sauces. The soup continues to bubble while the group serves themselves from the surrounding plates and bowls, chatting and eating. The segment ends with the grill still active, plates of meat and sauce arrayed on the table, and additional bowls of ingredients beside the hot plate.

You evaluate YouTube videos for a video-understanding benchmark.

You will be given an Action100M-style summary of one video: title, description,
a hierarchical GPT-written summary of the whole video, and a deduplicated list
of action labels extracted at multiple levels of the video.

Your job is to judge:

1) DOMAINS — does this video clearly belong to either of these target domains?
   - "kitchen": a person preparing food in a kitchen-like setting
     (cooking, baking, food prep — NOT eating reviews, NOT pet-food prep,
     NOT food-product unboxing, NOT restaurant vlogs).
   - "manipulation": a person performing hand-object manipulation tasks
     with clear physical goals: assembly/disassembly, repair, crafting,
     tool use, packing, sorting. The video must show clear procedural
     manipulation, NOT just incidental hand movement (e.g. a vlog where
     someone holds things while talking does NOT count).
   A video can match neither, one, or both. Be strict — when in doubt,
   say "neither".

2) NUM_DISTINCT_EVENTS — count the number of *semantically distinct*
   sub-events (procedural steps) you see in the action list. Merge
   paraphrases of the same step into one. Ignore generic narration steps
   like "speak to camera" or "display title".

3) IS_GOOD_CANDIDATE — true only if BOTH:
   - at least one target domain matches
   - num_distinct_events > 3 (the video shows a real multi-step procedure)

Always return strict JSON in the requested schema.
